lead: Water heated at constant pressure passes through three stages: liquid warms to saturation, liquid boils at fixed temperature, and steam superheats. The heat taken in each stage has a name and a symbol. Dryness fraction x tells how much of a wet mixture is vapour, so one number fixes enthalpy, volume and entropy between saturated liquid and saturated vapour. Boiler operators, turbine designers and examiners use these ideas to price steam, check coal use and avoid blade erosion.
prereq: You need: phase names and the p-v-T surface from 5.1, and enthalpy h = u + pv from the first law.

blocks.text: Heat 1 kg of water at 20 °C and 1 atm. The temperature rises to 100 °C. The heat added here is sensible heat, because it changes temperature. At 100 °C the water is a saturated liquid: liquid at its boiling point for that pressure. Its specific enthalpy is h<sub>f</sub> = 419 kJ/kg. Specific enthalpy h = u + pv (kJ/kg) adds the specific internal energy u to the flow work pv, pressure times specific volume.

More heat at 1 atm does not raise the temperature. Water boils into vapour at 100 °C. This hidden heat is the latent heat of vaporisation h<sub>fg</sub>. At 1 atm h<sub>fg</sub> = 2257 kJ/kg. Most of it pulls the molecules apart (u<sub>fg</sub> ≈ 2087 kJ/kg); the rest, p·v<sub>fg</sub> = 101.325 × 1.672 ≈ 169 kJ/kg, pushes the atmosphere back as the volume grows. Neither part raises the temperature, so the thermometer stays at 100 °C. When the last liquid disappears, the state is saturated vapour, with h<sub>g</sub> = 2676 kJ/kg. Further heat gives superheated steam: steam above its saturation temperature. At 150 °C the enthalpy is about 2776 kJ/kg.

blocks.where: h<sub>f</sub> is the specific enthalpy of saturated liquid (kJ/kg); h<sub>g</sub> is the specific enthalpy of saturated vapour (kJ/kg); h<sub>fg</sub> is the latent heat of vaporisation (kJ/kg). At 1 atm, 2257 = 2676 − 419.

blocks.text: Wet steam is saturated liquid and saturated vapour together. Dryness fraction x is the mass fraction that is vapour. Some syllabi call x quality; a percentage must be divided by 100 before use.
m<sub>g</sub> is the mass of vapour (kg); m<sub>f</sub> is the mass of liquid (kg); x is the dryness fraction, no unit. x = 0 is saturated liquid; x = 1 is saturated vapour; 0 < x < 1 is wet steam.

Take 1 kg of wet steam. It contains x kg vapour and (1 − x) kg liquid. The liquid part carries h<sub>f</sub> per kg. The vapour part carries h<sub>fg</sub> above h<sub>f</sub> per kg. So the mixture enthalpy is a straight-line rule between the two saturation values.

blocks.where: h is the specific enthalpy of wet steam (kJ/kg); x is dryness fraction; h<sub>f</sub> and h<sub>fg</sub> are taken at the same pressure. For m kg, total enthalpy H = m h (kJ).

blocks.text: Specific volume v and specific entropy s follow the same linear rule, because each is a mass-weighted property in the wet region.
v = vf + x (vg − vf) and s = sf + x (sg − sf)
v is specific volume (m³/kg); s is specific entropy (kJ/(kg·K)); subscript f means saturated liquid; subscript g means saturated vapour.
At 10 bar the latent heat 2015 kJ/kg is smaller than 2257 kJ/kg at 1 atm. Higher pressure pushes the liquid and vapour states closer.

A T-v sketch shows a saturation dome. Under the dome is wet steam. A constant-pressure line is horizontal while boiling, and v grows steadily from v<sub>f</sub> to v<sub>g</sub> as x goes from 0 to 1. A T-h sketch has a sloped liquid line, a flat boiling line of length h<sub>fg</sub>, and a sloped superheat line. The flat line is short at high pressure and disappears at the critical point.

The critical point is about 22.1 MPa and 374 °C for water; see 5.2. There hfg = 0, so there is no latent heat and no flat boiling line. Liquid and vapour have the same density. Below the critical point, hfg falls as pressure rises: 2257 kJ/kg at 1 atm, 2015 kJ/kg at 10 bar, zero at critical.

An h-s sketch is the Mollier diagram. In the wet region, lines of constant x lie under the saturation curve. Reading the chart is a skill for 5.5. A throttling calorimeter finds x from a measured temperature, as 5.6 shows. Vapour power cycles use these same numbers; they are taught with the cycles.

figure.caption: Steam formation at constant pressure on a T-h plot. At 1 atm the flat boiling line is 2257 kJ/kg long; at 10 bar it starts higher, at 179.9 °C, and is shorter, 2015 kJ/kg. The first worked example’s wet steam, x = 0.9 at 1 atm, sits at h = 2450.3 kJ/kg.

spec.aria: Temperature against enthalpy for water heated at 1 atmosphere and at 10 bar. Each line rises through the liquid, runs flat while boiling, and rises again as superheated steam. The boiling line at 10 bar is shorter and higher than at 1 atmosphere.

examples.question: 2 kg of wet steam at 1 atm has dryness fraction 0.9. At 1 atm h<sub>f</sub> = 419 kJ/kg and h<sub>fg</sub> = 2257 kJ/kg. Find the specific enthalpy h, the total enthalpy H, and the masses of liquid and vapour.
steps: Write the data: m = 2 kg, x = 0.9, h<sub>f</sub> = 419 kJ/kg, h<sub>fg</sub> = 2257 kJ/kg.
Use the wet-steam rule: h = h<sub>f</sub> + x h<sub>fg</sub> = 419 + 0.9 × 2257.
The latent part is 0.9 × 2257 = 2031.3 kJ/kg. So h = 419 + 2031.3 = 2450.3 kJ/kg.
Total enthalpy: H = m h = 2 × 2450.3 = 4900.6 kJ.
Mass of vapour: m<sub>g</sub> = x m = 0.9 × 2 = 1.8 kg.
Mass of liquid: m<sub>f</sub> = m − m<sub>g</sub> = 2 − 1.8 = 0.2 kg. Check: (1 − x)m = 0.1 × 2 = 0.2 kg.
examples.answer: The specific enthalpy is 2450.3 kJ/kg, the total enthalpy is 4900.6 kJ, and the mixture contains 1.8 kg vapour and 0.2 kg liquid.
examples.check:
m = 2.0
x = 0.9
hf = 419.0
hfg = 2257.0
h = hf + x * hfg
H = m * h
mg = x * m
mf = m - mg
print(round(h, 1))
print(round(H, 1))
print(round(mg, 1))
print(round(mf, 1))

examples.question: 2 kg of water at 25 °C (h = 104.8 kJ/kg) is pumped into a boiler at 10 bar and turned into steam. At 10 bar, T<sub>sat</sub> = 179.9 °C, h<sub>f</sub> = 763 kJ/kg, h<sub>fg</sub> = 2015 kJ/kg and h<sub>g</sub> = 2778 kJ/kg. Find the heat supplied when the steam leaves (a) wet with x = 0.9, (b) dry saturated, (c) superheated to 250 °C, taking c<sub>p</sub> of superheated steam as 2.1 kJ/(kg·K). Ignore the pump work.
steps: At constant pressure the heat supplied per kg is the rise in enthalpy: q = h<sub>final</sub> − h<sub>water</sub>, and Q = m q.
(c) Degree of superheat = 250 − 179.9 = 70.1 K. h = h<sub>g</sub> + c<sub>p</sub> (T − T<sub>sat</sub>) = 2778 + 2.1 × 70.1 = 2778 + 147.2 = 2925.2 kJ/kg.

Check against the superheated table: at 10 bar and 250 °C it gives h = 2943 kJ/kg. The c<sub>p</sub> estimate is 18 kJ/kg (0.6 per cent) low, because c<sub>p</sub> of steam is larger near saturation; use the table when one is given.
examples.answer: (a) 4943.4 kJ, (b) 5346.4 kJ, (c) 5640.8 kJ with the c<sub>p</sub> estimate (5676 kJ with the table value 2943 kJ/kg).

traps: Using h<sub>fg</sub> without multiplying by x: for x = 0.9 the latent part is 0.9 × 2257 = 2031.3 kJ/kg, not 2257 kJ/kg.
Reading 90% quality as x = 90. Divide by 100 first, so x = 0.90.
Using h = x h<sub>g</sub> in the wet region. h<sub>g</sub> already contains h<sub>f</sub>; the correct rule is h = h<sub>f</sub> + x h<sub>fg</sub>.
Mixing specific and total quantities: h is kJ/kg, H = m h is kJ. A 2 kg sample multiplies by 2.
Using h<sub>f</sub> + x h<sub>fg</sub> for superheated steam. Superheated steam needs the steam-table value at its pressure and temperature.

quiz.q: Define dryness fraction. State its range and the meaning of x = 0 and x = 1.
quiz.a: x = m<sub>g</sub>/(m<sub>f</sub> + m<sub>g</sub>). Range 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. x = 0 is saturated liquid; x = 1 is saturated vapour.

quiz.q: Why does the temperature not rise while water boils at 1 atm?
quiz.a: At fixed pressure the phase change occurs at the saturation temperature. The heat supplied becomes latent heat, breaking liquid bonds, so it does not raise temperature until all liquid becomes vapour.

quiz.q: Wet steam at 1 atm has x = 0.85, h<sub>f</sub> = 419 kJ/kg and h<sub>fg</sub> = 2257 kJ/kg. Find h.
5 kg of wet steam at 10 bar has x = 0.92. Take h<sub>f</sub> = 763 kJ/kg and h<sub>fg</sub> = 2015 kJ/kg. Find the total enthalpy H.
At the critical point h<sub>fg</sub> = 0. What does this mean for boiling and for the flat part of a T-h sketch?
quiz.a: There is no latent heat. Liquid changes continuously to vapour without a constant-temperature boiling stage, so the flat line shrinks to a point and h<sub>f</sub> = h<sub>g</sub>.

beyond: Not for the exam. In power plants, steam leaves a boiler slightly wet, and droplets can erode turbine blades, so operators measure dryness and often add superheat. Above the critical pressure a boiler has no boiling flat part, and the plant is called supercritical. Search for steam dryness fraction, turbine erosion, and IAPWS-IF97 steam properties for industrial data.
